key_terms.meaning: Legal upper limit on each pollutant per km of a fixed driving cycle: CO, HC, NOx and PM in g/km, PN in particles/km
India's emission stages, based on the Euro ladder; BS IV from 2017, BS VI from April 2020 (BS V skipped)
λ = AFR ÷ AFR<sub>st</sub> = AFR ÷ 14.7 for petrol; λ = 1 stoichiometric, λ < 1 rich, λ > 1 lean
Oxidises CO and HC and reduces NOx at once, only in a window about 1 % wide at λ = 1 and above light-off (about 250 to 350 °C)
Exhaust gas recirculation: inert exhaust fed back to the intake lowers peak flame temperature and so NOx
Fuel mass per km × about 3.16 kg CO₂ per kg petrol; fixed by fuel used
P = 2πNT ÷ 60, with N in rev/min, T in N·m, P in W
Brake work per cycle ÷ swept volume; four-stroke: 4πT ÷ V<sub>d</sub>
ṁ<sub>f</sub> × 1000 ÷ P in g/kWh (ṁ<sub>f</sub> in kg/h, P in kW); lower is better
Output from stored maps only / output corrected from a measurement of the result (the oxygen sensor)
Table of calibrated values (pulse width, spark advance) indexed by speed and load, read by linear interpolation
ṁ<sub>air</sub> = η<sub>v</sub> × ρ × V<sub>d</sub> × N ÷ 2, with ρ = p ÷ (RT) from manifold pressure and temperature
Fuel per injection ÷ injector flow, plus the dead time
Short-term: live correction from the oxygen sensor; long-term: learned offset stored against speed and load
θ<sub>d</sub> = 0.006 × N × t<sub>d</sub> crank degrees (N in rpm, t<sub>d</sub> in ms)
Spark fires at min(θ<sub>MBT</sub>, θ<sub>knock</sub> − margin) degrees BTDC

takeaways: Each emission stage lowers the ceiling per km for every pollutant, and one pollutant over its ceiling fails the vehicle.
λ = AFR ÷ 14.7 decides the exhaust: CO and HC rise rich, NOx peaks slightly lean, and only λ = 1 lets a hot three-way catalyst clean all three.
Power = 2πNT ÷ 60, BMEP = 4πT ÷ V<sub>d</sub> and BSFC = fuel flow ÷ power are the test-cell numbers behind every calibration choice.
An ECU reads sensors, interpolates maps and drives actuators; it is closed loop only where a sensor measures the result.
Speed density turns manifold pressure and temperature into air mass, then fuel per injection, then an injector pulse plus dead time.
The oxygen sensor only trims the base pulse: short-term trim hunts around λ = 1, long-term trim learns slow drift.
Dwell time is held for coil energy, so dwell angle grows with speed; the spark fires at the lesser of MBT and the knock limit minus a margin.
Knock control retards fast and advances slowly; misfire detection reads crank speed and reports.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask long answers on the chain sensor → ECU map → actuator, and on the effect of air-fuel ratio, spark timing and EGR on emissions, power and BSFC as the reason for electronic control. Calculation questions usually ask for brake power, BSFC, efficiency, injector pulse width or dwell angle.

bank.q: Define brake specific fuel consumption, relate it to fuel mass flow and brake power, and explain why BSFC is a better yardstick than fuel flow alone. Show how the ECU's injector data gives the fuel flow.
outline: BSFC = fuel mass flow ÷ brake power, in g/kWh
Brake power from torque and speed: P = 2πNT ÷ 60
Fuel flow from fuel per injection × injections per second
Two engines with the same fuel flow but different power are not equally efficient
Link to brake thermal efficiency; the low-BSFC island at moderate speed and fairly high load
answer: Definition. Brake specific fuel consumption is the mass of fuel an engine burns for each unit of work it delivers at the crankshaft: BSFC = ṁ<sub>f</sub> ÷ P. With ṁ<sub>f</sub> in kg/h and P in kW, BSFC = ṁ<sub>f</sub> × 1000 ÷ P in g/kWh. Lower is better.
Brake power. A dynamometer measures torque T (N·m) at speed N (rev/min). One radian of rotation at torque T does T joules, so P = T × ω = 2πNT ÷ 60 watts.

answer.text: Fuel flow from the ECU. The ECU knows the fuel it injects: fuel flow = fuel per injection × injections per second. For the four-cylinder engine of the fuel-control example at 3000 rpm:
answer.pre:
fuel per injection = 26.83 mg
injections per second = 4 cylinders × 3000 ÷ 120 = 100
fuel flow = 26.83 mg × 100 = 2.683 g/s = 2.683 × 3600 ÷ 1000 = 9.659 kg/h

answer.text: BSFC at that point. If the dynamometer reads 40.0 kW brake power there:
Why fuel flow alone misleads. Two engines on the test bed each burn 11.5 kg/h:

answer: The fuel flows are equal, but A turns each gram into 18 % more work (287.5 ÷ 244.0 = 1.18). Fuel flow describes how much the engine drinks; BSFC describes what each gram buys. That is why engines of different size, speed and load are compared by BSFC, and why it is directly tied to efficiency: η<sub>bth</sub> = 3600 ÷ (BSFC × CV), so halving BSFC doubles efficiency.

BSFC across the map. BSFC changes with the operating point. At high speed friction and pumping grow; at light load the fixed losses and throttling loss are large against the small brake power; at full load the ECU enriches the mixture. So the low-BSFC island sits at moderate speed (about 2000 to 3000 rpm) and fairly high load. Typical best values are about 230 to 260 g/kWh for petrol and about 200 g/kWh or less for diesel.
Check. Engine A: 244.0 × 47.12 ÷ 1000 = 11.50 kg/h, the measured flow, so the BSFC is consistent.

bank.q: Explain the working of a three-way catalytic converter and why the engine must be held near λ = 1 for it to work.
outline: Construction: honeycomb, washcoat, platinum, palladium, rhodium
Oxidation of CO and HC and reduction of NOx happen together
Narrow window around λ = 1; rich leaves CO and HC, lean leaves NOx
Closed-loop control with the oxygen sensor hunts across λ = 1; oxygen storage
Light-off temperature and the cold-start problem
answer: Construction. A ceramic (or metal) honeycomb of many thin channels sits in a steel shell in the exhaust. The channel walls carry a porous washcoat (mainly alumina, with ceria for oxygen storage) that spreads the precious metals: platinum and palladium speed oxidation, rhodium speeds the reduction of NOx. The honeycomb gives a large surface with little back pressure.

answer.text: Reactions. Three conversions happen on the same surface:
answer.pre:
CO oxidation:  2CO + O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub>
HC oxidation:  C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>m</sub> + (n + m/4) O<sub>2</sub> → n CO<sub>2</sub> + (m/2) H<sub>2</sub>O
NOx reduction: 2NO + 2CO → N<sub>2</sub> + 2CO<sub>2</sub>

answer: Why λ = 1. The oxidation needs oxygen; the reduction needs a gas with no spare oxygen (CO, HC and hydrogen take the oxygen away from NO). Only near the stoichiometric mixture, λ = 1, does the exhaust carry both in balance. Lean of the window (λ > 1) the spare oxygen leaves NOx unreduced; rich of it (λ < 1) there is too little oxygen to burn all the CO and HC. The window is only about 1 % wide in λ.

How the ECU holds it. The switching oxygen sensor upstream of the catalyst reads about 0.8 to 0.9 V rich and 0.1 V lean. The ECU ramps the injector pulse leaner until the sensor flips lean, then richer until it flips rich, so the mixture hunts around λ = 1 about once or twice a second. Ceria in the washcoat stores oxygen on the lean swings and gives it back on the rich swings, which smooths the hunt. A second sensor after the catalyst checks that this storage still works.

answer.text: Numbers (engine fuelling example). Engine-out CO 8.0, HC 1.2, NOx 1.0 g/km, catalyst hot:

answer: A 2 % lean drift lifts NOx from 0.05 to 0.40 g/km, 6.7 times the limit. That is the whole case for closed-loop electronic fuel control.

Light-off. The catalyst converts little until it reaches its light-off temperature, about 250 to 350 °C. After a cold start the first minute can carry much of a short trip's emissions, so the ECU retards the spark to send hot exhaust to the catalyst, some engines add secondary air, and catalysts are mounted close to the engine.

Limits of the device. A three-way catalyst cannot work on a diesel or a lean-burn engine (always λ > 1), lead and high sulphur poison it, and overheating from misfire (raw fuel burning in the catalyst) can melt the honeycomb.

bank.q: Distinguish open-loop and closed-loop fuel control. State when the ECU uses each, and how it switches between them.
outline: Open loop: fuel from stored maps only, no feedback
Closed loop: the oxygen sensor trims the injection time
The sensor switches at λ = 1; short-term and long-term trims
Open loop at cranking, warm-up, full load, deceleration and on sensor failure
Conditions to enter closed loop
answer: Open loop. The ECU reads speed and load, interpolates the base injection time from its calibrated map, adds corrections (coolant temperature, battery voltage for dead time, acceleration) and fires the injector. Nothing measures what burned, so any error in air measurement, fuel pressure or injector flow passes straight to the exhaust.

Closed loop. The exhaust oxygen sensor measures the result. A switching zirconia sensor gives about 0.8 to 0.9 V rich and 0.1 V lean, crossing at λ = 1 (the ECU uses about 0.45 V as the switch point). The ECU compares it with the target and corrects the base pulse with a trim, so the mixture is held at λ = 1 whatever the drift.

answer.pre:
open loop:   speed, load → map → pulse → injector → engine
closed loop: speed, load → map → (pulse × (1 + trim)) → injector → engine → O<sub>2</sub> sensor
                                      ↑_________________ compare with λ = 1 ____________|

answer: Trims. Short-term fuel trim is the live correction: the ECU ramps the pulse leaner until the sensor reads lean, then richer until it reads rich. When short-term trim stays biased (say +8 %), the ECU stores that offset as long-term trim for that speed and load, so the next drive starts from the corrected pulse.

head: Condition
Mode
Why
rows: sensor below its working temperature (about 300 °C); cold enrichment
rich (λ about 0.85 to 0.9) for power and to cool valves and catalyst
injectors off; no fuel to control
no valid feedback; base map plus long-term trim

answer: Switching in. The ECU enters closed loop only when all are true: coolant above a threshold (about 40 to 60 °C), the oxygen sensor has been switching (it is hot), a set time has passed since start, and the operating point is not full load or deceleration. It leaves closed loop as soon as one fails, for example when the throttle opens fully.

Comparison. Open loop is fast (no waiting for exhaust to reach the sensor) but trusts the calibration. Closed loop corrects wear, altitude and fuel differences but reacts only after the gas reaches the sensor, which is why the base map must already be close: the trim corrects only a few percent.

bank.q: Explain the speed-density method of estimating the air trapped in a cylinder, and use it to find the fuel per injection.
outline: Inputs: manifold absolute pressure, intake air temperature, speed, volumetric efficiency map
Ideal gas law gives manifold air density
Air mass per cylinder per cycle = η<sub>v</sub> × ρ × swept volume per cylinder
Fuel per injection = air ÷ AFR; then pulse width
Limits: needs recalibration for cam or intake changes; contrast with mass airflow sensing
answer: Idea. The ECU cannot see the air in the cylinder, but it can measure what fills it: the manifold absolute pressure (MAP) p and the intake air temperature T. The ideal gas law gives the manifold air density, and a calibrated volumetric efficiency η<sub>v</sub> says how much of the swept volume is actually filled at that density.

answer.pre:
ρ = p ÷ (R T),                     R = 287 J/(kg·K)
air per cylinder per cycle = η<sub>v</sub> × ρ × V<sub>cyl</sub>
ṁ<sub>air</sub> (whole engine) = η<sub>v</sub> × ρ × V<sub>d</sub> × N ÷ 2       (N in rev/s, four-stroke)
fuel per injection = air per cylinder ÷ AFR

answer: η<sub>v</sub> is not constant: it depends on speed and throttle, so it is stored as a map against speed and MAP, filled on the dynamometer. "Speed" in the name is the engine speed that indexes this map and sets the number of cycles per second.

answer.text: Full load (fuel-control example: 1.6 L, four cylinders, V<sub>cyl</sub> = 0.4 L, 3000 rpm, MAP 100 kPa, 27 °C, η<sub>v</sub> = 0.85):
answer.pre:
ρ = 100 000 ÷ (287 × 300) = 1.161 kg/m³ (use 1.16)
air per cylinder = 0.85 × 1.16 × 0.0004 = 0.000394 kg = 394.4 mg
fuel per injection = 394.4 ÷ 14.7 = 26.83 mg
flow time at 3.0 g/s = 26.83 ÷ 3.0 = 8.94 ms; with 0.9 ms dead time, 9.84 ms

answer.text: Part load (same engine, MAP 50 kPa, 27 °C, η<sub>v</sub> = 0.75 from the map):

answer: The manifold pressure halves and η<sub>v</sub> falls, so the air (and the fuel) falls to 174.2 ÷ 394.4 = 44 % of the full-load value. MAP is therefore the ECU's main load signal.

Strengths and limits. Speed density needs only a robust MAP sensor and a temperature sensor, so it is cheap and does not restrict the intake. But its accuracy rests on the η<sub>v</sub> map: a different camshaft, a leaking EGR valve, variable valve timing or a modified intake changes the real η<sub>v</sub> and the ECU will not know. A mass airflow (hot-film) sensor measures the air directly and follows such changes, at higher cost; many engines carry both and cross-check them.
Check. 0.85 × 1.16 × 0.0016 × 25 = 0.03944 kg/s for the whole engine, and 4 cylinders × 25 cycles/s × 394.4 mg = 39.44 g/s: the per-cylinder and whole-engine forms agree.

bank.q: Explain dwell and the electronic ignition control sequence for one cylinder, from crank signal to spark.
outline: Coil stores energy ½LI² while primary current flows; spark when switched off
Dwell time set by battery voltage; dwell angle grows with speed
Sequence: crank and cam signals, speed and load, advance map, corrections, dwell start, spark
Knock correction
Numbers from a timing example
answer: Coil energy. When the ECU's driver switches the coil primary on, current rises towards a limit set by the winding resistance and the driver. The energy stored is E = ½LI². When the driver switches off, the field collapses, the secondary (many more turns) produces tens of kilovolts and the plug arcs. With L = 4 mH and I = 7 A, E = 0.5 × 0.004 × 49 = 0.098 J = 98 mJ.

Dwell. Dwell time t<sub>d</sub> is how long the primary is on before the spark. Too short gives a weak spark (misfire); too long heats the coil. Because the current rise depends on battery voltage, the ECU reads t<sub>d</sub> from a voltage table: this is constant-energy ignition. Dwell angle θ<sub>d</sub> = 0.006 × N × t<sub>d</sub> degrees, so for a fixed dwell time the angle grows with speed.

answer.text: The sequence for one cylinder, each cycle:
answer.pre:
1. crank sensor teeth (and the missing-tooth gap) → crank angle and speed N
2. camshaft sensor → which cylinder is on compression
3. load from manifold pressure or air flow
4. base advance from the speed-load map (interpolated)
5. corrections: coolant, intake air, EGR, knock retard → final θ<sub>spark</sub>
6. dwell time from battery voltage → θ<sub>d</sub>
7. switch the coil on at θ<sub>spark</sub> + θ<sub>d</sub> BTDC
8. switch it off at θ<sub>spark</sub> BTDC → spark

answer.text: Worked timing (spark example: 3.0 ms dwell, spark 25° BTDC):

answer: Room between sparks. With one coil for four cylinders the sparks are 180° apart: 5.0 ms at 6000 rpm, enough for 3.0 ms dwell plus a 1.5 ms spark. At 8000 rpm the gap is 180 ÷ 48 = 3.75 ms, so the dwell must be cut to about 2.25 ms. Wasted-spark and coil-on-plug layouts give each coil 360° or 720°, which removes this limit.

Advance and knock. The final advance is the lesser of the MBT advance and the knock limit minus a margin. The knock sensor's signal, filtered and windowed after each spark, makes the ECU retard 2 to 4 degrees on knock and creep back slowly when it stops.
Check. At 6000 rpm, 133° BTDC to 25° BTDC is 108°, and 108 ÷ 36 = 3.0 ms, the commanded dwell.

bank.q: Trace how emission norms tightened from BS IV to BS VI (Euro 4 to Euro 6) and state what each step demands from the engine management system.
outline: Limits in g/km for CO, HC, NOx, PM (and PN) over a fixed driving cycle on the whole vehicle
BS IV and BS VI values for petrol and diesel cars; India skipped BS V
Petrol demands: closed-loop λ control, precise spark, catalyst heating, OBD
Diesel demands: high-pressure injection, EGR, SCR, particulate filter
Why mechanical control cannot meet these limits
answer: How limits are set. A stage gives a ceiling for each pollutant in g/km (PN in particles/km), measured on the complete vehicle over a fixed driving cycle on a chassis dynamometer. Every pollutant must be under its ceiling. Each Euro stage lowered the ceilings; India followed as Bharat Stage, with BS IV across the country from April 2017 and BS VI from April 2020, skipping BS V. Fuel sulphur fell from 50 to 10 ppm with BS VI.

answer.text: The step from BS IV to BS VI for cars (g/km):

answer: Petrol demands. CO and HC stayed, but NOx fell 25 %, and a three-way catalyst must clean all three. That needs λ held within about 1 % of 1 at all times: closed-loop fuel control with oxygen sensors before and after the catalyst, sequential injection, accurate air measurement and adaptive trims. Fast catalyst light-off needs spark retard after cold start. Direct-injection engines must also meet a particle number limit, which needs injection timing control or a particulate filter.

Diesel demands. NOx fell from 0.25 to 0.08 g/km and PM by 82 %. A diesel runs lean, so it cannot use a three-way catalyst; the ECU must run common-rail injection at high pressure with several injections per cycle, cooled EGR, selective catalytic reduction with urea dosing, and a particulate filter whose regeneration the ECU schedules.

Monitoring. The second BS VI phase (from April 2023) added on-road (real driving) emission checks and stricter on-board diagnostics, so the ECU must monitor its own catalyst, sensors, EGR and misfire and store fault codes.

Why electronics. A carburettor and a mechanical distributor drift with wear, temperature and altitude and cannot hold λ = 1 within 1 % or measure their own result. Each tighter stage therefore moved more of the engine under ECU control.
Check with numbers. The engine-fuelling example car makes 0.11 g/km NOx: 137.5 % of the BS IV limit and 183.3 % of BS VI, so the NOx cut alone fails it, even though its CO (82 %) and HC (70 %) pass.

bank.q: A four-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine runs at 3000 rev/min at light load with a measured air mass flow of 30 kg/h and λ = 1 (stoichiometric ratio 14.7). It has sequential injection, so each injector fires once per cycle. Fuel density is 750 kg/m³. Each injector flows 2 g/s when open and has a dead time of 0.9 ms. Find the fuel flow, the mass and volume of fuel per injection, the commanded pulse width and the injector duty.
outline: Fuel flow = air flow ÷ 14.7 = 2.04 kg/h
Injections per second = 4 × 3000 ÷ 120 = 100
Fuel per injection = 5.67 mg = 7.56 mm³
Flow time = 2.83 ms; commanded pulse = 3.73 ms
Duty = 3.73 ÷ 40 = 9.3 %; comment on dead time and battery voltage
answer: Fuel flow. At λ = 1 the air-fuel ratio is 14.7, so fuel flow = 30 ÷ 14.7 = 2.041 kg/h.

Injections per second. Speed = 3000 ÷ 60 = 50 rev/s; a four-stroke cycle takes two revolutions, so each cylinder has 25 cycles a second. With one injection per cylinder per cycle: 4 × 25 = 100 injections per second.

answer.pre:
fuel flow = 2.041 kg/h ÷ 3600 = 0.000567 kg/s = 0.567 g/s
fuel per injection = 0.567 g/s ÷ 100 = 0.00567 g = 5.67 mg
volume = 5.67 × 10⁻⁶ kg ÷ 750 kg/m³ = 7.56 × 10⁻⁹ m³ = 7.56 mm³

flow time = 5.67 mg ÷ 2 g/s = 0.00567 g ÷ 2 g/s = 2.83 ms
commanded pulse = flow time + dead time = 2.83 + 0.90 = 3.73 ms

answer: Duty. One cycle at 3000 rpm lasts 2 × 60 ÷ 3000 = 0.040 s = 40 ms. Duty = 3.73 ÷ 40 = 0.093, that is 9.3 %. The injector is open for less than a tenth of the cycle, which leaves plenty of room at higher loads.

Dead time and battery voltage. Here the dead time is 0.9 ÷ 3.73 = 24 % of the pulse, so a dead-time error matters most at light load and idle, where pulses are short. The opening delay grows when battery voltage falls (the coil current rises more slowly), so the ECU reads the dead time from a battery-voltage table every injection.

answer.text: Why the dead time must follow battery voltage. Suppose the battery falls to about 10 V and the true dead time grows to 1.3 ms, but the ECU still commands 3.73 ms:
answer.pre:
real flow time = 3.73 − 1.30 = 2.43 ms
fuel delivered = 2.43 ms × 2 g/s = 4.86 mg (needed 5.67 mg)
fuel ratio = 4.86 ÷ 5.67 = 0.857, so λ ≈ 1 ÷ 0.857 = 1.17: 14 % short of fuel, lean
correct command = 2.83 + 1.30 = 4.13 ms

answer: A 17 % lean mixture is far outside the three-way catalyst window (about 1 %), so NOx would pass straight through and the engine might hesitate. The oxygen sensor would eventually pull the trim back, but the battery-voltage table fixes it before the first injection.

Comparison. In the full-load fuel-control example the same kind of engine needed 26.83 mg per injection; at this light load it needs 5.67 mg, about a fifth, because the air flow (30 kg/h = 8.33 g/s against 39.44 g/s) is about a fifth.
Check. 5.67 mg × 100 per s × 3600 s/h = 2.04 kg/h, the fuel flow we started from.

bank.q: An engine of 2.0 L swept volume develops 60 kW brake power at 4000 rev/min and consumes 18 kg of petrol per hour. Calculate the brake torque, BMEP, BSFC, fuel power and brake thermal efficiency. Take the calorific value of petrol as 43 MJ/kg.
outline: BMEP = 4πT ÷ V<sub>d</sub> = 9.0 bar
BSFC = 18 000 g/h ÷ 60 kW = 300 g/kWh
η<sub>bth</sub> = 60 ÷ 215 = 27.9 %, checked by 3600 ÷ (BSFC × CV)

answer.text: BMEP. A four-stroke completes one cycle in two revolutions, so the work per cycle is 2π × 2 × T = 4πT:

answer.pre:
ṁ<sub>f</sub> = 18 kg/h ÷ 3600 = 0.005 kg/s
fuel power = 0.005 kg/s × 43 000 kJ/kg = 215 kW

answer.text: Going further. With petrol density 0.74 kg/L and an assumed mechanical efficiency of 0.85:
answer.pre:
fuel volume = 18 ÷ 0.74 = 24.3 L/h
indicated power = 60 ÷ 0.85 = 70.6 kW; friction power = 70.6 − 60 = 10.6 kW
indicated thermal efficiency = 70.6 ÷ 215 = 0.328 = 32.8 %

answer: If a car needed this output to cruise at 120 km/h, it would use 24.3 ÷ 120 × 100 = 20.3 L/100 km, which shows why cruising power is kept far below 60 kW in practice: a small car needs about 15 to 20 kW at that speed.

Comment. 300 g/kWh is well above a good petrol best point (about 230 to 260 g/kWh), so this point is off the low-BSFC island: 4000 rpm adds friction, and if this is near full load the ECU is enriching. Of every 215 kW of fuel energy, only 60 kW reaches the shaft; the other 155 kW goes to coolant, exhaust and friction. BSFC and efficiency move inversely: 3600 ÷ (BSFC × CV) halves when BSFC doubles.

bank.q: Explain how the ECU uses the knock sensor to protect the engine, and show with a step-by-step trace how spark timing changes when knock appears.
outline: Knock: self-ignition of end gas; ringing at 5 to 15 kHz
Piezo accelerometer; band-pass filter, knock window after each spark, threshold
Retard 2 to 4 degrees at once; advance slowly after clean firings
Retard limit; then enrich or cut boost
Trade-off: retard raises exhaust temperature and BSFC
answer: Knock. After the spark, the flame front compresses the unburnt end gas ahead of it. If that gas reaches its self-ignition temperature it explodes all at once, giving a sharp pressure spike that rings the cylinder at a frequency set by the bore (typically 5 to 15 kHz). Heavy knock erodes pistons and cracks ring lands within seconds.

Sensing. A piezoelectric accelerometer bolted to the block produces a charge proportional to vibration. The ECU band-pass filters the signal around the knock frequency, looks only in a window of crank angle after each spark (so valve closing noise is ignored), rectifies and integrates it, and compares it with a threshold that rises with engine speed. A reading above the threshold is a knock event for the cylinder that just fired.

answer.text: Trace. Base map advance 28° BTDC; knock limit at this load about 24°; retard 3° per knock event; advance 1° after each run of clean firings:

answer: The timing settles in a band just under the knock limit (about 22 to 24°) and hunts there. Fast retard and slow advance keep it stable: one heavy knock can damage the piston, while a slow return only costs a little torque for a few seconds.

Limits. Retard is capped (often about 10 to 15 degrees below the map). If knock continues at the cap, the ECU enriches the mixture (fuel evaporation cools the charge) and, on a turbo engine, cuts boost. The learned retard is stored, so the next time the engine meets this point it starts nearer the limit, for example after a tank of low-octane petrol.

Cost. Running 4 to 6 degrees below MBT moves the pressure peak late, so torque falls and BSFC rises a few percent; the exhaust is hotter. That is the price of 91-octane fuel in an engine calibrated for 95.
Check. The settled band (22 to 24°) is below the knock limit minus no margin (24°), and the step size (3°) is larger than the creep step (1°), as the loop requires.

bank.q: Describe how air-fuel ratio affects exhaust emissions, fuel economy and power, and explain how the controller chooses the mixture at cold start, idle, part load, full load and deceleration.
outline: Rich: CO and HC up, NOx down, power up, economy down
Lean: CO low, HC rises again very lean, NOx peaks slightly lean, economy better until misfire
λ = 1 closed loop at part load for the three-way catalyst
Enrichment at full load and cold start; fuel cut on deceleration
Trade-off sketch of emissions against λ
answer: Measure. λ = AFR ÷ 14.7 for petrol. λ < 1 is rich (excess fuel), λ > 1 lean (excess air).

Sketch: on a λ axis from 0.8 to 1.2 draw CO falling steeply to the lean side, HC with its minimum slightly lean and rising at both ends, NOx peaking near λ = 1.06, and a narrow band at λ = 1 marked "three-way catalyst window".

Cold start. The fuel condenses on cold port walls, so the ECU injects much more than λ = 1 would need (cranking enrichment from a coolant table), then tapers it as the engine warms. The oxygen sensor is cold, so this is open loop. CO and HC are high and the catalyst is below light-off, so the ECU retards the spark to heat it.
Idle. Once warm, idle runs at λ = 1 in closed loop; the idle air valve or electronic throttle holds the speed and the spark is nudged for fine control.

Part load and cruise. Most driving is here, so this is where emissions and economy are decided. The ECU holds λ = 1 in closed loop for the three-way catalyst, and adds EGR to cut NOx and throttling loss. Lean burn would save fuel but the three-way catalyst could not reduce NOx, so stoichiometric engines do not use it.

Full load. The driver wants power. The ECU leaves closed loop and enriches to about λ = 0.85 to 0.9: maximum power and lower exhaust temperature, which protects valves, turbocharger and catalyst. CO and HC rise for the short time this lasts.

Acceleration and deceleration. A sudden throttle opening gets a short extra pulse (fuel wets the port walls); closing the throttle above about 1500 rpm cuts fuel completely, which saves fuel and avoids HC from a too-lean mixture.
Number check. At the 13.2 : 1 acceleration mixture of the engine fuelling example, λ = 13.2 ÷ 14.7 = 0.90: rich, as the full-load row says.

bank.q: Compare carburetion with electronic petrol fuel injection on mixture accuracy, cylinder-to-cylinder distribution, emissions, cold starting and transient response.
outline: Carburettor meters by venturi depression; drifts with temperature, wear and altitude
Injection meters by open time per cylinder from measured air
Port injection gives equal distribution; transients need wall-wetting compensation
Cold start and altitude from maps and sensors
Why BS VI cannot be met with a carburettor
answer: How each meters fuel. A carburettor accelerates air through a venturi; the pressure drop draws fuel through a fixed jet, so fuel follows air only as well as the venturi curve allows. Electronic injection measures or computes the air (speed density or mass airflow), computes the fuel and opens an injector for a calculated time at a regulated pressure (about 3 to 4 bar above manifold pressure).

head: Aspect
Carburettor
Electronic port injection
rows: drifts with air density, fuel temperature, jet wear; no feedback
closed loop holds λ within about 1 %
MAP and air temperature correct it automatically
one mixture shared through the manifold; end cylinders differ
one injector per cylinder, equal fuel
fuel still drawn at idle jet

answer: Mixture accuracy in numbers. The engine fuelling example shows what a 2 % lean drift does at the catalyst: tailpipe NOx rises from 0.05 to 0.40 g/km, 6.7 times the BS VI limit. A carburettor routinely drifts by more than 2 % with temperature and altitude, so it cannot hold the window.

Electronic carburetion. Fitting a feedback solenoid to a carburettor gave λ near 1 at steady cruise and was a stop-gap; it could not fix distribution, cold start or transients, so it gave way to injection.

Fuel economy and power. Injection needs no venturi, so the intake can be larger (higher volumetric efficiency, more power), and the fuel cut and precise cruise mixture save fuel. The fuel-control example shows the ECU computing 26.83 mg per injection to within the injector's resolution.

Evaluation. For any engine sold under BS VI, injection is the only practical choice: the limits need closed-loop λ control, catalyst heating and on-board diagnostics, none of which a carburettor can provide. The carburettor survives only where emission rules are loose, such as some small off-road engines.
Check. The comparison rests on one number: the three-way catalyst window, about 1 % in λ, is narrower than a carburettor's drift.

bank.q: Evaluate the effect of EGR on NOx, knock, combustion stability and fuel consumption, and explain how the ECU meters EGR.
outline: NOx forms at high peak temperature; EGR dilutes the charge and lowers it
Moderate EGR reduces throttling loss and knock, allowing more advance
Too much EGR slows the burn, raises HC, causes misfire
Little or none at idle and full load
Metering: stepper or vacuum valve, position feedback, MAP check; cooled EGR
answer: Why NOx forms. NOx forms when nitrogen and oxygen combine at the highest flame temperatures (above about 2000 K), and its rate rises steeply with temperature. Cutting peak temperature by even a little cuts NOx a lot.

What EGR does. Exhaust gas is mostly N<sub>2</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O, which do not burn. Mixed into the charge, it absorbs heat (CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O have high heat capacity) and dilutes the oxygen, so the flame is cooler and slower. Typical part-load EGR rates of 10 to 20 % cut engine-out NOx substantially.

head: Effect
Moderate EGR at part load
Too much EGR
rows: reduced (cooler end gas), so more advance is allowed
slower; ECU adds advance (the EGR correction in the spark table)
little change or slightly better: less throttling, less heat loss

answer: Why fuel use need not rise. To make the same torque with exhaust in the charge, the throttle must open wider, so manifold pressure rises and the pumping loss falls. Cooler gas also loses less heat to the walls. These gains roughly offset the slower burn, so the net effect at part load is small or slightly positive.

Where EGR is shut. At idle the burn is already unstable, so EGR would cause misfire. At full load every bit of oxygen is wanted for power. During cold start the burn is too slow. The ECU therefore schedules EGR from a speed-load map, with zero in these regions.

Metering. The EGR valve is either a stepper-motor or DC-motor valve (position sensed by a potentiometer) or a vacuum diaphragm switched by a solenoid. The ECU commands a position from its map and checks the result: the valve position sensor, and a rise in manifold pressure when the valve opens (or a change in mass air flow, which drops because exhaust replaces fresh air). A stuck valve sets a diagnostic code.

Cooled EGR. Passing the exhaust through a coolant-cooled heat exchanger makes it denser and cooler, so more can be added for the same volumetric efficiency penalty and knock falls further; downsized turbo petrol engines and all modern diesels use it.

Verdict. EGR is the cheapest in-cylinder NOx control for a petrol engine and costs little fuel when it is metered by the ECU and kept away from idle and full load. Its limit is combustion stability, so the calibration finds the largest rate that still burns smoothly at each point.

bank.q: A car has a fault in the manifold absolute pressure sensor. Analyse how the ECU detects the fault and what fallback strategies keep the car running.
outline: Circuit checks: signal out of range high or low (open, short to ground or supply)
Plausibility: compare with throttle angle, speed, a model or the air-flow sensor; key-on reading against barometric pressure
Fallback: substitute load from throttle and speed (alpha-N) or a default value
Open-loop fuel, safe spark advance, EGR off, limited speed
Warning lamp, fault code, freeze-frame data read over the diagnostic link
answer: The sensor. A MAP sensor is a piezoresistive bridge on a silicon diaphragm with a reference vacuum on one side. It gives a voltage that rises with absolute pressure, typically about 0.5 V at very low pressure to 4.5 V near atmospheric, from a 5 V reference. The ECU uses it as its main load signal for fuel (speed density) and spark.

head: Reading
Likely fault
Detection
rows: open signal wire or short to ground
out of range low for a set time
short to the 5 V reference or open ground
no change while the throttle moves

answer: Plausibility checks (signal in range but wrong). With the key on and the engine stopped, the MAP must read barometric pressure (about 100 kPa at sea level); a reading of 60 kPa is implausible. At idle with the throttle closed a healthy engine pulls about 30 to 40 kPa; at wide-open throttle about atmospheric. The ECU also compares MAP with a model built from throttle angle and speed, and, if fitted, with the mass air-flow sensor. A persistent mismatch is a fault even though the voltage is in range.

Fallback load. Once a fault is confirmed, the ECU stops using the sensor and computes a substitute load from throttle angle and engine speed (the alpha-N method, using a stored table), or at worst a fixed default value. Air density is then estimated from the intake temperature and the last known barometric pressure.

head: System
Fallback
rows: base pulse from the substitute load; closed-loop λ trim kept if the oxygen sensor is healthy, which corrects much of the load error
a safe, retarded map so that knock is unlikely
warning lamp on; the car can be driven to a workshop (limp-home)

answer: Recording. The ECU stores a diagnostic trouble code (for example, MAP circuit high) with freeze-frame data: speed, coolant temperature, throttle angle and trims at the moment of the fault. A technician reads them through the on-board diagnostic connector, which talks to the ECU over the CAN bus.

Evaluation. Detection must avoid false alarms, so each check needs the fault to persist for a set time or number of cycles. The fallback trades emissions and performance for safety: the car keeps moving, the engine is protected by the retarded spark, and the oxygen sensor still limits the mixture error. A speed-density engine without a backup load signal is the worst case, which is why many engines cross-check MAP against the throttle.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of an engine management system and explain the role of each block, including the in-vehicle network and diagnostics.
outline: Inputs: crank, cam, MAP, air temperature, throttle, coolant, oxygen, knock
ECU: signal conditioning, ADC and timer inputs, processor with flash, RAM and EEPROM, driver stages
Outputs: injectors, coils, idle air valve, EGR valve, purge valve, fuel pump relay
Closed loops: λ through the oxygen sensor; idle speed; knock
CAN bus to other ECUs; diagnostics and limp-home

svg.aria: Engine management system block diagram: eight sensors feed an ECU of signal conditioning, ADC and timer inputs, processor with memory and driver stages; six actuators; exhaust feedback to the oxygen sensor; CAN bus to other ECUs.

answer.text: Input sensors and what they tell the ECU:

head: Sensor
Measures
Used for
rows: timing of every injection and spark; misfire
cold enrichment, idle speed, closed-loop entry

answer: Signal conditioning. Scales each sensor voltage into the ADC range, filters noise from the ignition and alternator, and clamps spikes. Pulse signals (crank, cam) are squared into clean edges.
ADC and timer inputs. A 10-bit ADC with a 5 V reference resolves 5 ÷ 1024 = 4.9 mV per count. Timer inputs time the gap between crank teeth to get speed and angle to a fraction of a degree.

Processor and memory. The microcontroller runs the program from flash memory, keeps live values in RAM and stores learned trims and fault codes in EEPROM or flash. Each cycle it interpolates the maps: in the concept example, 2000 rpm and 46 kPa give a 5.2 ms base pulse. It adds corrections and works out when, in crank degrees, to switch each output.
Driver stages. Low-side power transistors switch the injectors and coils, with clamps for the inductive kick; others drive stepper motors (idle air, EGR) and relays (fuel pump).

head: Actuator
Controlled quantity
rows: fuel mass by open time (for example 9.84 ms at full load in the fuel-control example)
dwell and spark angle (3.0 ms dwell, 25° BTDC in the spark example)
Idle air valve or electronic throttle
fuel supply; off if the engine stalls

answer: Closed loops. Three loops run inside the system: the λ loop (injectors → combustion → exhaust → oxygen sensor → trim), the idle speed loop (idle valve → speed from the crank sensor), and the knock loop (spark → knock sensor → retard). Everything else is open loop from maps.

Network and diagnostics. The engine ECU shares speed, torque, throttle and fault data over the CAN bus with the transmission ECU (shift timing, torque reduction during shifts), the ABS and traction control ECU (torque cuts when a wheel spins) and the body and instrument ECUs (gauges, warning lamps). The on-board diagnostic system monitors sensors, catalyst, EGR and misfire, stores fault codes with freeze-frame data, lights the warning lamp, and switches to limp-home values when a sensor fails. A scan tool reads all this through the diagnostic connector.

Summary. Sensors measure, the ECU decides from calibrated maps, actuators act, and three feedback loops correct the result. The network lets the engine cooperate with the rest of the car, and diagnostics keep the whole chain honest over its life.

glossary.def: Mass of air divided by mass of fuel entering the engine; about 14.7 for complete combustion of petrol.
Actual air-fuel ratio divided by the stoichiometric ratio; 1 means chemically correct.
The mixture in which all the fuel can burn using all the oxygen supplied.
The catalyst temperature at which conversion reaches about half; about 250 to 350 °C.
The fraction of a pollutant entering the catalyst that it removes.
A converter that oxidises CO and HC and reduces NOx together when the mixture stays near λ = 1.
A valve that admits a metered fraction of exhaust gas into the intake to lower combustion temperature.
Brake power divided by the heat energy supplied by the fuel per second.
Brake mean effective pressure: brake work per cycle divided by swept volume.
Air actually trapped in the cylinder divided by the air that would fill the swept volume at manifold conditions.
Pressure in the intake manifold measured from vacuum; the ECU's main load signal in speed density.
A two-dimensional table of calibrated values indexed by engine speed and load.
Filling the ECU tables from dynamometer and road tests so the engine meets emission, power and driveability targets.
The computer that reads the sensors, runs the maps in real time and drives the actuators.
A solenoid valve that sprays fuel; the quantity is set by its open time and the pressure difference across it.
The time in milliseconds the ECU holds an injector open.
The opening delay of an injector, about 0.5 to 1 ms, added to every pulse and longer at low battery voltage.
The ECU's correction to injection time from the oxygen sensor: short-term (live) and long-term (learned).
The time (or crank angle) the ignition coil primary is switched on before the spark.
The crank angle before top dead centre at which the spark occurs.
Minimum spark advance for best torque.
Self-ignition of the end gas ahead of the flame, giving a sharp pressure rise and a metallic ringing.
An inductive or Hall-effect sensor reading a toothed wheel to give crank angle and speed.
A fallback in which the ECU uses substitute values and limits the engine so the car can reach a workshop.
A stored code identifying which monitored circuit or system has failed.
A two-wire broadcast bus with message identifiers and arbitration that lets vehicle ECUs share data.
The official approval test a new vehicle model must pass before it can be sold.
